text: Egyptian blue is the oldest known synthetic pigment, in use in Egypt around 3000 BCE. Under infrared light it glows, which lets scientists find traces of it on ancient statues.
In the Middle Ages ultramarine came only from the lapis lazuli mines of Badakhshan in Afghanistan; pigment from there travelled more than 6,000 km to reach Germany.

More than 100 particles of ultramarine were found in the dental plaque of an 11th-century woman buried at a German monastery. The likeliest reason: she licked her brush to a fine point while painting manuscripts.
In 1775 Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered a bright green pigment made with arsenic. It ended up in wallpapers, dresses and book covers.
Some 19th-century green bookcloth carries about 1.42 milligrams of arsenic per square centimetre. The advice is to handle such books with nitrile gloves.
On 11 September 1841 John Goffe Rand patented collapsible metal paint tubes with a screw cap, which made painting outdoors far easier.
Indian yellow was said to come from the urine of cows fed only on mango leaves. The story is plausible and chemically consistent, but has never been confirmed or debunked.
Prussian blue was found by accident in Berlin around 1706, the first modern synthetic pigment. It reached Edo, now Tokyo, in 1829.
Hokusai began Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, the series that includes the Great Wave, in 1830, when he was 70 years old.
Claude Monet owned 250 Japanese prints, 23 of them by Hokusai.
Museum visitors at the Art Institute of Chicago spent a mean of 28.63 seconds in front of each artwork, and the most common time was just 10 seconds.
The rule of thirds began in 1797 as advice about light and shade, not about where to put things in a picture.
The woman in van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait is almost certainly not pregnant: holding up a full skirt was simply the fashion.
Rembrandt's Night Watch was cut down on all four sides when it moved to Amsterdam's town hall in 1715. In 1975 a visitor slashed it with a bread knife.
The Night Watch measures 379.5 by 453.5 centimetres, Rembrandt's largest canvas. It hangs in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.
Van Eyck did not invent oil painting. Oil-based murals at Bamiyan in Afghanistan date from the 7th century.
When a German newspaper printed a reconstruction of a painted Greek statue in 2001, readers were indignant at the vivid colours. Greek marble was painted all along.
Abbot Suger rebuilt his abbey church at Saint-Denis between 1137 and 1148, creating the model for the Gothic cathedral. 'Gothic' itself began as an insult.
In 1917 Marcel Duchamp signed a urinal with a false name and entered it in a New York exhibition. In 2004, 500 art experts voted it the most influential work of modern art.
Did Duchamp really choose Fountain? Some historians credit the Baroness Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven, citing a letter Duchamp wrote to his sister. Others point to Louise Norton's own account.
Maurizio Cattelan's Comedian, a banana taped to a wall, sold in 2024 for $6.2 million with fees, after a seven-minute bidding war.
Five of Warhol's Campbell's soup can canvases first sold for $100 each. The gallery's co-owner, Irving Blum, then bought them back so the set could stay together.
In the Nazi purge of 'degenerate art' in 1937, fifty-seven of Kandinsky's works were confiscated.
Hilma af Klint began radically abstract paintings in 1906, years before Kandinsky, Malevich and Mondrian, who usually get the credit.
The Mona Lisa was not even the most famous painting in its own gallery in 1911. Its theft that year made it a global celebrity.
Thieves took 13 works from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in 81 minutes in 1990. They are now worth at least half a billion dollars, and the frames still hang empty.
The Salvator Mundi sold at Sotheby's in 1958 for £45 as a work by Leonardo's assistant. In 2005 dealers bought it for $1,000 plus commission; in 2017 it sold as a Leonardo for $450 million.
Cadmium yellow was introduced around 1800, so when it turned up in a still life sold as a Zurbarán, who died in 1664, the attribution collapsed.
Radiocarbon can date oil paint to the decade: in one forgery the linseed oil came from seeds harvested in 1958–61 or 1983–89, thanks to the bomb pulse.
In 1650 the dying collector Wu Hongyu tried to have the scroll Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains burned. His family saved it, but it survived in two pieces.
In the Kimberley, scientists dated Aboriginal rock paintings using tiny amounts of carbon in mud wasp nests built over and under the paint.
Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri's Warlugulong was bought in 1977 for $1,200 and hung in a staff canteen for some 20 years. It later sold for millions.
London's Horniman Museum transferred ownership of 72 Benin objects in November 2022, sent six back and keeps the rest on loan.
The only surviving Aztec feather headdress of its kind, made in the early 16th century, is in Vienna. Conservators counted at least 170 breaks in its 374 long quetzal feathers.
